items.transcript: It just 3 weeks ago, it felt like nothing could go wrong. The SpaceX was up 7% in a day. Every tech CEO in America was on stage explaining why they needed another 100 billion dollars to decimate farmland and rule America. And Jensen Huang was telling anyone who listened that demand for AI chips was insatiable. But since then, the market took a dump. Meta created an entirely new class of non-voting stock just to pay for GPUs, while Microsoft offered a quarter of its employees money to leave so it can afford more of them. Elon predicted that 200 Neo clouds are about to experience guppy level death. And CoreWeave, a former Ethereum mining operation that became the poster boy of reckless AI spending after they pivoted into renting Nvidia GPUs back to Nvidia, is now worth a third of what it was at the beginning of the month. And then on Monday, Anthropic filed to go public, which showed that between January and when the government banned Fable back in June, they lost more money than the annual GDP of over half the countries on Earth. So naturally, the question on everyone's mind is are we finally cooked? In today's video, we'll break down 3 weeks in the history of AI, find out what a Neo cloud is and why Elon wants them dead, and we'll analyze Anthropic's financials in their trust-me-bro S-1. It is October 28th, 2026, and you're watching The Code Report. But before we can talk about the AI bubble, you need to understand how a GPU actually gets paid for. And to do that, here's me in a bubble bath to explain. But first, Nvidia makes a GPU that they need to sell. The problem is the GPU is expensive, and you don't have enough money to buy it. So Nvidia says, "Hey, we have money and we'll give it to you as long as you give us a portion of your company and use the money we give you to buy our GPUs." But Nvidia's money only covers a fraction of what you need. So you go to Wall Street and borrow the rest by putting up the GPU you haven't bought yet as collateral. Now, normally, a bank wouldn't lend to you with a depreciating pile of chips as collateral, but Nvidia has promised that if nobody rents the GPUs they give you, they'll rent them themselves. So Nvidia's money gets used to buy Nvidia GPUs that eventually get rented back to Nvidia, which makes Nvidia stock go up, which it uses to invest in more companies, which borrow more money to buy more Nvidia GPUs, which keeps the good times going. On Wall Street, they call this a circular financing arrangement, and back in college, we'd call it a The most popular company eating this forbidden fruit is CoreWeave, but Nvidia has done it with a few other companies as well. And to be honest, it works pretty well as long as the chips rent for more than they depreciate. The labs keep buying, and someone keeps lending you money to buy more chips. But 3 weeks ago, the third one stopped being true when it was discovered that CoreWeave, after it borrowed $52 billion to buy chips, was now paying 15% interest on that debt. Then on Sunday night, Elon chimed in saying that debt markets have almost entirely shut off for any company whose only revenue is AI data centers, and that he expects 200-plus of these neo-cloud type companies to die. But conveniently, SpaceX is fine because it also happens to sell rockets. And right in the middle of all this, Anthropic decided to ask the public for $100 billion at a valuation that would make it worth more than 492 out of the 500 companies in the S&P 500, with four out of those seven remaining companies being where they rent their compute from, and happen to owe $265 billion to through 2045. The S-1 itself is 330 pages long, with 90 of those being risk factors to the company, which is the fun part. In it, Anthropic admits that everything we've already covered over the last few months is true, including Mythos being allergic to its sandbox, a Claude Haiku filing a fake homicide tip through the Philadelphia Police Department's website, and a Chinese state-sponsored group using Claude code to attack banks and government agencies. The filing also says that Claude now uses itself to improve itself, and that they might not notice their models getting significantly smarter until after it's already happened. Their guiding principle, according to the forward, is to under-promise and over-deliver, which is a little worrisome for a company whose head of alignment was quoted just last month saying he thinks there's a greater than 10% chance that AI kills all humans within the next decade. So, are we cooked? Well, as always, it depends. It's not looking great if your whole business model is borrowing money from one company just to give it right back to them. But, it's hard to call AI a bubble the day after OpenAI claims one of its models disproved a 27-year-old conjecture that half of complexity theory is built on. But, thankfully, as developers, things are actually looking pretty decent right now since every one of these companies are fighting to sell us subsidized tokens. Ikemi just dropped an open model within a point of Opus at half the price that we talked about yesterday. And the GPUs core we financed should be on eBay any week now. And if you'd like to be one of the people profiting from the exit liquidity instead of providing it, you can put those subsidized tokens to work with Hyperagent, the sponsor of today's video. If you're already paying for ChatGPT, you can now use that plan to sign into Hyperagent and hire a team of agents without setting up yet another AI subscription. Right now, I'm using it to work on a V4 release of a date library I'm contributing to. So, I set up a Hyper agent room, which is basically a Slack channel where all my agents and human co-maintainers can work together. I've got one agent triaging new issues as they come in, another one drafting pull requests for new features, and a third one writing the change log. They all work in parallel and hand things off to each other and only ping a human when something needs approval. And anyone on a team can jump in to ask questions or make changes whenever they want instead of routing everything through me. Sign in with your existing ChatGPT plan to try it out at the link below. This has been the Code Report. Thanks for watching, and I will see you in the next one.

items.transcript: Last week an anonymous mystery model named Kibitz showed up randomly on Sha Bot Arena performing at the frontier level. A Kibitz is the Yiddish word for that guy standing behind you at a chess game and giving you tips on how to blunder your queen, which to be honest is the perfect analogy for a coding agent. But it was pretty obvious he was behind this mystery model from the beginning because the first two letters of this word are a dead giveaway. Everybody knew it was Kimmy. Then right on cue last Friday, Moonshot dropped Kimmy K 3.1 officially giving us a new 3 trillion parameter open weight model that will be fully downloadable on November 4th, or so they say. And just when you thought the AI bubble was popping and the trust me bro benchmarks could not possibly get any better, Kimmy made them better. >> I can go lower. >> In today's video, we'll find out why Kimmy K 3.1's performance should be impossible and put it to the test on the only benchmark that matters, building 3D horses with 3.js. It is October 26, 2026 and you're watching the Code Report. Earlier this year, Anthropic accused Moonshot AI, the company behind Kimmy, alongside a bunch of other Chinese companies like Deep Seek and Mini Max of running large-scale distillation attacks against Claude by sending swarms of fake users to steal Claude's output and reasoning tokens, which could then be used to train these open models that they give to us for free. Now, I believe distillation is a fundamental human right because big AI companies have literally distilled the collective human brain by taking our internet web logs, our GitHubs, our scientific papers, and they even destructively scanned our books without asking. Just Google Project Panama. But Open AI and Anthropic don't really see distillation as a human right like I do. To them it's Grand Theft Auto Complete and they've invested millions and millions of dollars into stopping it. And just a few weeks ago, Anthropic said it pretty much solved the distillation problem with 90 to 99% of distillation attacks from China now being blocked. And over at Open AI, they've proved that their tech can even stop small-scale distilleries like PewDiePie. But if that's true, that means an open Chinese model with Kimmy's performance should not be possible because for years big AI has insinuated that that the reason Chinese models get so good so fast is that they steal big AI's outputs. But if we can trust this trust me bro distillation data from Anthropic, that would mean that these trust me bro benchmarks from Kimi should not be possible. Like Kimi K3.1 is within one point of Opus 5.5 on Terminal Bench 4.0. That's pretty crazy and no other open model is remotely close. And we might even be able to actually trust these numbers because artificial analysis ran it independently and got 67% which is the highest score of any model they tested. But one thing to keep in mind is that the harness plays a big role here. Running different models with different harnesses will produce huge differences in benchmark results. In addition, Kimi also wins on SWE marathon which is a test for multi-hour software requirements. Or in other words, jobs that would take humans weeks of work to finish without AI assistance. That's all pretty impressive, but there is one big caveat when it comes to coding and specifically cybersecurity. Moonshot deliberately ripped out a bunch of cybersecurity data from its training data set where the goal was to make the model even worse at hacking than pirate software. >> I'm a genius, dude. >> And it worked because internally at Moonshot an unfiltered checkpoint solved 90.5% of their illegal exploit tests. But the final release model only solves 81% and that's a smart business move on their part because just a few days ago the US banned China's deep seek model from government use including all federal civilian agencies. And they would just love a good reason to ban all Chinese models across the board to hand Open AI and Anthropic a huge win and make all the insiders even more unbelievably rich than they already are. And that's why Moonshot really has no choice but to lobotomize its hacking capabilities. But despite that, Kimi still performed on top of all publicly available models on the new cyber index at artificial analysis. Although that's mostly because Claude and GPT-6 declined every prompt on safety grounds and just took the L. But nowadays, the only AI capability that I really care about is how well it can generate a 3D horse with 3js. And to analyze the skill objectively and scientifically, I use a formal benchmark. It's a state-of-the-art eval I've developed after thousands of hours of research, which I call thoroughbench. The way it works is I literally just go into the chat window and type create a realistic interactive 3D horse with 3js and then press enter. From there, I rank them from 0 to 10 based on a proprietary loss function I keep in my brain. Using this technique, Google Argon achieved a 0.69, a GPT-6 Astra achieved a 5.21, and Opus achieved a 6.39. But now it's time to try Kimi K3.1. I tried to be cheap and use the free tier, but got denied. So now I'm paying 250 yuan per month to show you guys this demo. It was worth it, though, because Kimi produced what is easily the most beautiful horse in this sample. It's coloring is spot on, it looks realistic, and most importantly, its copulatory organ is a reasonable size. I was blown away by its beauty at first glance, but then I push play on the animation and found a problem. The animations are absolutely terrible. If we look closely, you can see it achieves the animation by simply warping the original mesh, which is a very unsophisticated and half-assed way to animate a 3D object. If we compare that to Claude, the horse itself may not look as beautiful, but it actually built a mesh with 95,000 vertices with each shape tied to one of 35 bones, and all those bones are animated independently. Even Gemini Argon used bones, but for some reason it added an extra one. A skeletal animation is more difficult, but it's why the horse doesn't look like it's being torn apart by a black hole when it walks. So the final score for Kimi K3.1 on thoroughbench is a 4.20, which is pretty dang impressive, but still behind the other frontier models. But if you really want to build an amazing 3D horse or user interface, you need to check out Mobbin, the sponsor of today's video. I've been using Mobbin for over 5 years, and its MCP server now lets your coding agent study its library of 600,000 real UI screens before it designs anything. So instead of asking for a login page and getting the same purple gradient vibe slop, you start by telling Claude, Code, Cursor, or Codex to study how the best apps built that complete user flow. It'll use Mobbin to gather references and build a visual report of the patterns they all share. Then, it'll recreate that flow and adapt it to your app. Every result points back to the original screen, so you can check the source. And after you connect Mobbin, everything your agent designs will feel like it has actual taste. But, try Mobbin for free today and get a 20% discount at the link below. This has been the Code Report. Thanks for watching, and I will see you in the next one.

PHP2Shell, a backdoored Python package with 23 million weekly downloads, a GitLab bug dating back to 2014, rogue AI agents inside bank accounts, and a certificate authority generating HTTPS keys from numbers under 256 — let's break down the craziest week in the history of the internet.

items.author: Fireship
items.transcript: It feels like it was just yesterday when the biggest risk to your infrastructure was the jaded Silicon Valley developer going manic and deleting his package from the NPM registry. But nowadays, it's a bit more bleak. In just the last 72 hours, the literal NSA encouraged anyone using PHP to go dark, a Python package with 23 million weekly downloads got backdoored, a GitLab found a bug that's been affecting every release since 2014, the US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agents operating inside customer accounts, and an Indian certificate issues HTTPS certificates for the entire internet was generating private keys with a 2D 100. In today's video, we'll break down the most vulnerable week in the history of the internet and once again look at how to update your infrastructure fast enough to not get zero-dayed, but slow enough to not get supply chain attack. It is October 23rd, 2026 and you're watching The Code Report. PHP stands for Personal Homepage and was created in 1994 by a Danish guy named Rasmus Lerdorf who admitted he actually hates programming. Just like me. Since then, PHP has been co-opted by the elite who love to flaunt their lavish lifestyles with no regard for the working class developer. Well, this week the joke's on them because PHP finally did some wealth distribution of its own when two bugs, now known as PHP 2 Shell, let anyone with an internet connection run whatever they want on any PHP server released in the last decade by stringing together two flaws in how PHP manages memory. The first one comes from the fact that every PHP server has a memory limit and when a request goes over it, it uses an old C trick to jump straight to the end of the request without finishing or cleaning up anything it was working on. The second one comes from the fact PHP recycles the same process for every request and the last one left in memory doesn't always get cleared before the next one arrives. For 20 years, neither of those was a problem, but recently researchers figured out that if you combine them by pushing PHP over its memory limit at exactly the right moment, like halfway through a file upload, it'll leave behind half-baked data that the next request can pick up and use, which if exploited means anyone can run their own code on your server. And this vulnerability was actually found a few months ago by a security firm using GPT 5.6 Soul, who brought it up with the PHP team, who then spent the last few months working on a fix that was supposed to drop yesterday. But that plan fell apart on Monday when the bug's ID leaked on Hacker News, and then the same firm who found it accidentally posted a video of themselves exploiting it on Tuesday. So that left 24 hours where the exploit was public, but the patch wasn't. The ramifications of which I'm sure we'll be hearing about for years to come. But that was only the beginning. On Wednesday, Node.js shipped a fix for a bug that lets an attacker run code on your server by sending it a malformed compressed file. And GitLab fixed one in the regex engine it bundles from Ruby that let anyone run code on a self-hosted server that's been there since 2014. Thankfully, if you just stay up-to-date on your dependencies, you'll be fine. Unless one of them is a Python library that most AI apps use to talk to models called Light LLM, where on Wednesday a new version shipped that stole any important credential on your machine and was up for a couple of hours before PyPI pulled it. But at least all of those hacks required some state-of-the-art models stringing together esoteric vulnerabilities. In this next one, it was just pure organic human incompetence. Every time your browser shows you an HTTPS lock, it's because a certificate authority confirmed that the website you're looking at is who it claims to be. That whole system depends on each authority keeping a handful of private 384-bit randomly generated keys secret. But last Saturday, a researcher noticed that eight of the keys belonging to an Indian certificate authority that's trusted by every major browser were integers smaller than 256, which in practical terms meant that anyone could start impersonating any website on the internet by simply guessing a number between 1 and 255 and then issuing a valid HTTPS certificate. eMudhra, the company responsible for the incompetence, blamed a bug in their key generation script, and I blame them for thinking that a 384-bit meant that you could pick a number between 1 and 384. Chrome, Firefox, Apple, and Microsoft all blocked the certificates within 3 days of discovering the issue, and Mozilla pulled one of eMudhra's root certificates out of Firefox entirely. And to finish off the week, Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan, and Bank of America say they've been finding agents logged into customer accounts doing things the customer never asked for. And this tracks because OpenAI recently disclosed that two of its own coding agents decided it was morbin' time and turned off alerts to its security team, removed their own monitoring, and when one was asked about it, it acted like nothing happened. >> It wasn't me. >> And all of this was sandwiched between two breaches that were both targeting the same thing. Last Friday, someone broke into OpenCode looking for users' OpenAI and Anthropic API keys, which OpenCode says was part of a large-scale distillation attack. And this week, Railway had to pause every customer deployment after attackers decrypted some customers' environment variables, which Railway says was also part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Which in a way is kind of a relief because no one wants your data anymore, just your API keys. But if you want help protecting your own projects, check out Semgrep, the sponsor of today's video. Everyone is slapping the words Mythos class on their security tools right now. So, Semgrep actually ran Mythos GPT Soul and a bunch of other frontier models through their own vulnerability benchmarks, and they found that the harness makes a much bigger difference than the model. The Semgrep's harness correctly identified 6.5 times as many real security bugs as the same model on its own because it gives the LLM real program analysis with data flow and dependency context. And their Guardian tool puts that inside your coding agent to protect it from itself. One command lets you install it as hooks and an MCP server, and every file your agent writes gets scanned right after it's written. Like here, Claude Code just tried to hardcode my live Stripe key, but Guardian blocked it before it touched Git, and the agent fixed it on its own. And it can do the same for vulnerable patterns and malicious packages right as they happen. The try Guardian for free for 60 days using the link below, which is double their normal trial. This has been the Code Report. Thanks for watching, and I will see you in the next one.
